place: Zini Gediği (Zini pass), Munzur mountains, Erzîngan (Erzincan)
impact: Victims' families exiled to western provinces; the site stayed a restricted zone and bones lay unburied until a memorial tomb in 2014
summary: During the Dersim campaign, Alevi Kurdish villagers from Surbahan (Kılıçkaya), Balıbey, Girlevik, Kismikor and Mağaçur were held under soldiers' guard, marched up to the Zini pass at about 3,200 m and killed there. BirGün gives 95 dead and bianet nearly 100; bianet dates the killings to 8 August 1938, other accounts to 6 August. In 2011 the Erzîngan prosecutor refused to prosecute, citing the statute of limitations.

impact: Remains never returned; the site is still a military zone
summary: On the orders of Third Army commander General Mustafa Muğlalı, soldiers executed 33 Kurdish villagers from the Serav (Saray) and Qelqelî (Özalp) districts, accused of 'border violation', on the banks of the Sefo stream; bianet reports one man survived. Muğlalı was sentenced to death in 1950, commuted to 20 years. The killings are remembered as '33 bullets' after Ahmed Arif's poem.

impact: Officers acquitted in 2006 on 'legitimate defence'; Turkey later paid €350,000 to seven families before the ECtHR
summary: Turkish special operations police opened fire with heavy weapons on a silent march of Kurdish villagers protesting village-guard recruitment and raids near Digor. Bianet gives the official toll of 17 killed, including children, and 63 wounded. The eight officers tried were acquitted, but before the ECtHR the Turkish government acknowledged that police used excessive force.

impact: Case reopened only in 2003; the captain named by the Court of Cassation is still a fugitive
summary: After a clash in which a soldier was killed, Turkish soldiers raided Vartinis and set fire to the house of the Öğüt family, stopping villagers from rescuing them; bianet reports nine people burned to death, seven of them children. Authorities first blamed the PKK, but Turkey's Court of Cassation found that gendarmerie captain Bülent Karaoğlu gave the order to burn the village.

summary: Turkish authorities imposed six curfews on Farqîn in two months, the longest from 3 November 2015. impact: First large Turkish air and ground incursion across the Turkish–Iraqi state border
summary: After a PKK attack at Çele (Çukurca), the Turkish state sent warplanes and about 8,000 troops across the Turkish–Iraqi state border against PKK camps, by Iraqi consent, as memurlar.net and TRT Haber recount. Wikipedia, citing Turkish press, lists 165 PKK fighters killed; no independent count was found and no civilian toll is recorded.

place: Qendîl (Qandil), Zap, Avaşîn, Metîna and Xakurkê
impact: UNHCR: about 1,800 villagers displaced; ten villages damaged, bridges and schools destroyed
summary: Turkish warplanes struck more than 200 targets in Qendîl, Zap, Avaşîn, Metîna and Xakurkê; the Turkish General Staff claimed 150–175 PKK fighters killed, while the PKK said it had no losses and Fırat News said seven people were killed. Local and Iraqi officials, reported by Al Jazeera and bianet, said at least one woman was killed and five or six civilians wounded; Turkey denied any civilian harm.

summary: In the ground and air incursion the Turkish state called 'Operation Sun', about 10,000 troops entered the Zap valley and Xakurkê. The figures were never independently verified; residents of border villages reported Turkish air strikes and shelling.

summary: Turkish warplanes bombed Qendîl and other areas of Kurdistan from 17 August 2011; on 29 August the Turkish General Staff claimed 'up to 160' PKK fighters killed (RFE/RL), and TRT later gave 270 for August–October. place: Baghdad, Xaneqîn (Khanaqin), Mendelî (Mandali) and Feyli areas
impact: 300,000–750,000 deported and stripped of citizenship under Decree 666 (7 May 1980); property seized
summary: From 4 April 1980 the Ba'ath state rounded up Feyli Kurds, stripped them of citizenship under Revolutionary Command Council Decree 666 of 7 May 1980 and expelled them to Iran; the KRG gives 300,000–500,000 deported and KGNA about 750,000. Thousands of young men were detained and disappeared: HRW (via VOA) says more than 10,000, Kurdistan24 10,000–20,000, KGNA about 23,000 and the KRG at least 25,000. The Iraqi High Criminal Court recognised the campaign as genocide in 2010.

impact: Hengaw verified 290 Kurds killed across Iran in the protests, including at least 23 children and 24 women
summary: Hengaw's first-half 2026 report verified the identities of 290 Kurds killed by Iranian state forces during the January 2026 protests, 284 of them by direct gunfire. Of these, 102 were killed in Kurdish provinces: 89 in Kirmaşan, 11 in Îlam and 2 in Kurdistan (Sine); most of the rest were killed in Tehran (92) and Alborz (36).
